title: Punch a wire down on a 110 block with the tool's cutting side toward the loose end
instruction: Punch the blue wire down into its contact on the 110 block with the punch-down tool, trimming off its loose end, then lift the tool off.
context: Cabling technicians terminate every conductor of a data or voice cable on 110 insulation-displacement blocks: the conductor is laid across its contact and a punch-down tool drives it into the contact's slot and shears the excess in one stroke. The blade cuts on one side only, marked CUT; the installer must face that side to the loose end. Reversed, the same stroke cuts the run off at the block, leaving a dead pair that has to be re-pulled or re-terminated short. Unlike #766 and #705 (open a lever or push-in clamp and insert a bare wire), here the contact displaces the insulation and the tool's facing decides which end is cut. Unlike #1205 (fire an automatic centre punch on a mark) and #741 (close a crimper on a held cable), the decisive act is turning the tool half a turn before the press, which nothing in the scene forces. Done by: telecommunications equipment installers; telecommunications line installers (O*NET 49-2022.00, 49-9052.00).
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left), all square to the table. A 110 wiring base (fixed, white polycarbonate, 4 x 6 x 1.2 cm) at x 27, y -24 carries a 4-pair connecting block: a 30 mm row, 6.4 mm deep, top 2.2 cm above the table, 8 insulation-displacement contacts (phosphor bronze) at 3.75 mm pitch between 3.3 mm plastic ribs. Each contact is two blade halves sprung shut to a 0.45 mm slot (2 N preload, 1,500 N/m each), with a 25 deg entry vee standing 2 mm above the plastic and a 1.0 x 0.9 mm groove under it. A blue 24 AWG solid conductor (0.51 mm copper, 0.9 mm PVC) lies across position 5 in the contact's vee: its run goes 15 mm back to a fanning-strip post, its loose end sticks 20 mm out over the front. A non-impact 110 punch-down tool (154 mm: steel blade and 7 mm shank, 20 x 24 x 100 mm ABS handle; 90 g) stands in a black ABS holster (4 x 4 x 4.5 cm, keyed blade pocket) at x 20.5, y -33.5. Its fork straddles the contact; on one side a cutting lip reaches 1.3 mm lower, passing 0.6 mm outside the block's edge; an orange stripe on the handle marks that side, which faces the back (the run) in the holster.
scoring: From the poses of the conductor's pieces, the contact halves and the tool (on a real rig: the conductor's depth in the slot, the contact's spread, which end is cut). Seated: the conductor's in-block length within 0.25 mm of resting on the groove floor, within 0.4 mm of the groove line and 1.5 mm of the contact along it, level within 6 deg, and both contact halves pushed open by at least 0.05 mm. Trimmed: the loose end parted from it at the block's front edge (driven 0.45 mm down across the edge by the blade, after which the joint parts). Run cut: the run parted at the back edge; latched for the trial, score 0. Score: 0.5 for seated; +0.3 if also trimmed; +0.2 if seated and the tool's tips are 5 mm above the block (or 15 mm away from the contact), both grippers 2.5 cm clear of the terminated conductor, and that conductor still (no piece moved over 0.5 mm or 1.5 deg across the last six scored poses; the cut-off scrap is ignored). Scored at the last step; 1.0 held for 1 s is success. Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 1.0.
reset_notes: Lay a new conductor across position 5 (a punched conductor cannot be re-used: its insulation is slit), with its run in the fanning strip and its loose end 20 mm out over the front, and stand the tool back in its holster with the CUT mark toward the back.
fidelity: Real sizes, rigid parts. Wire: four rigid 0.9 mm capsules; run joints bend plastically (0.002 N*m). Each wire piece weighs 3 g, about 30x real, with set inertia, because lighter pieces made the joints stretch. Cutting is a scripted strain break: a per-step rule parts the joint at a block edge once the blade has pushed the outer piece 0.45 mm down across it; PhysX force breaks never tripped. Contact: two sprung sliders. Non-impact tool: an impact tool's ~130 N trip is beyond the arm.
